A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BridgeVLA work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation evaluations, real-robot success rates, and a pre-training ablation in Section 4 and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds architectural ablations, real-robot baseline comparisons, and an inference-time measurement.

M1.justification: The proposed BridgeVLA architecture, heatmap pre-training, multi-view projection, action losses, and coarse-to-fine inference remain unchanged. The direct-regression and positional-feature variants introduced in Section 4.3 are experimental controls, not revisions to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use RoboPoint pre-training, RLBench, COLOSSEUM, GemBench, and the same 13 real-robot tasks with the same seven evaluation settings. Additional demonstrations for SpatialVLA change sample counts within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds SpatialVLA, π0, and ACT to the real-robot Basic comparison alongside RVT-2 (Table 4), substantially broadening comparison beyond the earlier RVT-2 and pre-training-ablation evaluation. Table 1 also adds direct-regression and positional-feature controls. The earlier pre-training comparator remains in Figure 3.

E3.justification: Basic-setting evaluation changes from five to ten trials per task (v1 Table 11; v2 Table 12). Added comparisons specify single-task ACT training, SpatialVLA budgets of 10 and 50 demonstrations, and capacity-matched regression controls with hyperparameter tuning. The original simulation protocols and BridgeVLA training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 4.3 tests two central architectural choices: heatmaps versus direct position regression, and excluding versus injecting per-pixel 3D position features. Appendix C.2 adds qualitative baseline failure analyses. The pre-training ablation and existing robustness and object-grounding analyses are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix A newly specifies that inference latency is averaged over 100 trials. Existing simulation repetition and seed counts, and their uncertainty-reporting practices, remain unchanged. Additional ablation rows reuse the existing reporting style; no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: New RLBench ablations report 31.4% and 56.2% versus retained BridgeVLA performance of 88.2%. Table 4 adds SpatialVLA results of 3.1%/28.5%, π0 at 3.8%, and ACT at 22.3%, versus BridgeVLA at 96.9%. Revised Basic counts yield 95.4% with three demonstrations under ten-trial evaluation, replacing v1's five-trial results; this is not a demonstrated same-setting performance loss. Average ranks change with the expanded Table 1 comparison, and Appendix A adds 0.21-second inference latency.

T1.justification: The policy and action definitions, truncated Gaussian heatmaps, normalization, and loss equations remain unchanged. New architectural explanations and empirical ablations introduce no formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The main contributions and claims of efficient manipulation through input-output alignment are retained. The abstract adds an explicit low-data comparison claiming that π0 fails completely. This strengthens the comparative claim, although Table 4 reports 3.8% success for π0 trained with ten demonstrations.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism and failure interpretation. Section 4.3 attributes heatmap benefits to denser supervision, spatial priors, and alignment, and interprets positional-feature degradation through feature-distribution shift. Appendix C.2 proposes explanations involving π0 overfitting and ACT's spatial generalization. Earlier limitations involving occlusion, long-horizon tasks, and unseen object categories remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds RTX 4090 inference hardware and timing information. Section 4.3 documents 309M versus 303M decoder sizes, the regression loss, positional-feature construction, and tuning details for the new controls. Existing BridgeVLA hyperparameters, freezing rules, training resources, and project access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work section is retained, while Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendix C.2 expand positioning against SpatialVLA, π0, and ACT in low-data learning. The CLIP reference is removed. The replacement π0 entry at reference 52 duplicates the work already cited as reference 6, rather than introducing a new unique cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract and real-robot discussion are rewritten, architectural ablations are grouped in new Section 4.3, and Appendix C gains a Basic Setting subsection. Appendix A is renamed to include inference details. These are localized narrative changes; most existing sections and explanations remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains two ablation rows and an expanded caption, and a new Table 4 displays real-robot baseline results. Existing tables and surrounding text reflow, including separation of the appendix COLOSSEUM tables across pages. All 14 figures retain their substantive visual content.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses two important evidential gaps in v1: direct real-robot comparisons with VLA methods and tests of the central heatmap and input-alignment design choices. Table 4 and Section 4.3 substantially strengthen support for the paper's data-efficiency and architectural claims. Reporting weaknesses temper this gain: the introduction retains 96.8% despite revised results of 95.4%, the RLBench prose retains an outdated rank, and the abstract overstates π0's failure. These inconsistencies do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.
